Chapter 186

Opioids

Tintinalli Ch.186 — opioid intoxication, naloxone, withdrawal, body packing

Jennifer S. Love, Jeanmarie Perrone

Thai EM BoardRosen'sATLS xABCDE

Introduction: Opioid Risk and ED Priorities

Opioids include natural opiates, semi-synthetic analgesics, synthetic opioids, fentanyl analogs, methadone, tramadol, meperidine, buprenorphine, heroin, and combination products. The board-facing ED priority is not the exact molecule first; it is ventilation failure. A patient with coma and bradypnea needs airway positioning, oxygen, BVM ventilation, glucose check, and naloxone targeted to breathing.

The classic triad is coma, miosis, and respiratory depression, but the full triad is not required. Hypoxia may dilate pupils; coingestants can alter mental status; and routine urine screens can miss fentanyl analogs or buprenorphine.

Tintinalli source check

Tintinalli Table 186-1. Major pharmaceutical opioids

Use this early to compare opioid potency, analgesic duration, and elimination half-life. It explains why methadone, buprenorphine, fentanyl, and sustained-release products can outlast naloxone.

High-yield trap: do not wait for urine toxicology before treating hypoventilation. Clinical physiology wins.

Mechanism and Toxidrome

Mu-opioid receptor activation reduces brainstem ventilatory response to carbon dioxide and causes dose-dependent sedation, analgesia, euphoria, bradycardia, hypotension, ileus, and miosis. Death is usually from respiratory depression with hypoxic injury.

Histamine release can occur with morphine and related agents, producing pruritus, flushing, and urticaria; this can look allergic but does not equal IgE anaphylaxis.

Tintinalli source check

Tintinalli Figure 186-1. Urticaria after IV morphine

Place this beside mechanism because it is a bedside differentiator: histamine-mediated urticaria can occur without true anaphylaxis.

Rosen source check

Rosen Box 135.4. Opioid intoxication vs withdrawal toxidrome

Rosen frames opioids inside the poisoned-patient toxidrome table: opioid intoxication is miosis, hypoventilation, and depressed mental status; withdrawal flips toward diarrhea, mydriasis, tachycardia, lacrimation, yawning, cramps, and piloerection.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli is more operational for naloxone dosing; Rosen strengthens the differential by contrasting opioid intoxication with cholinergic, anticholinergic, sedative-hypnotic, sympathomimetic, and withdrawal patterns.

Diagnosis and Differential

Diagnosis is clinical: abnormal ventilation, depressed mental status, opioid exposure risk, miosis or compatible pupils, and response to naloxone. Important mimics include clonidine/imidazoline toxicity, sedative-hypnotics, ethanol, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, intracranial hemorrhage, sepsis, carbon monoxide, and trauma.

Tintinalli source check

Tintinalli Table 186-2. False-positive urine opioid screens

Use this with the diagnostic section: screening tests can be misleading. Poppy seeds, quinine, diphenhydramine, dextromethorphan, and several medications may confuse opioid or methadone screens.

Rosen source check

Rosen poisoned-patient differential beside diagnosis

Use Rosen's toxidrome framing next to the diagnostic workup: opioid findings overlap with clonidine, sedative-hypnotics, ethanol, hypoglycemia, head injury, and mixed intoxication.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli gives opioid-specific management; Rosen forces a broader poisoned-patient differential when the response to naloxone is incomplete or the vital signs do not fit.
Rosen decision rule: if naloxone improves ventilation but fever, focal neurologic deficit, QRS widening, severe acidosis, or trauma signs persist, keep searching. Opioid exposure does not close the case.

Naloxone and Ventilatory Rescue

Naloxone reverses opioid receptor effects, but oxygenation and ventilation come first. In opioid-dependent patients who are breathing, start low and titrate to adequate ventilation. In apnea or cyanosis, give larger doses while bagging.

Tintinalli source check

Tintinalli Table 186-3. Naloxone by route

This table belongs in the treatment section, not only in Drug Dose Reference. Dose depends on the goal: gentle reversal in a breathing chronic user versus full reversal in apnea/cyanosis.

Naloxone endpoint

Target adequate respiratory rate, oxygenation, and airway protection; complete arousal is optional and sometimes harmful.

Renarcotization

Methadone, fentanyl patches, sustained-release opioids, buprenorphine, and body packets can outlast naloxone; repeated dosing or infusion may be needed.

Special Opioids and Exposure Patterns

Buprenorphine has high receptor affinity and may require higher or repeated naloxone dosing plus ventilatory support. Methadone has long duration and QT risk. Meperidine's metabolite normeperidine can cause seizures. Tramadol adds seizure and serotonergic risk. Fentanyl can cause abrupt apnea and chest wall rigidity.

Body packers intentionally transport many well-wrapped packets; asymptomatic packers typically need CT confirmation, whole bowel irrigation, and monitoring. Body stuffers hurriedly swallow fewer, poorly wrapped packets and still need observation for packet rupture. Endoscopic retrieval is dangerous because rupture can cause massive overdose.

Opioid Withdrawal

Withdrawal is the mirror image of intoxication: anxiety, yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, mydriasis, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia, and hypertension. It is usually not lethal in adults but causes major distress and return visits.

Tintinalli source check

Tintinalli Tables 186-4 and 186-5. Withdrawal features and COWS

Use the timing table to recognize withdrawal and COWS to grade severity before symptomatic treatment or buprenorphine initiation.

Board trap: buprenorphine before moderate withdrawal can precipitate withdrawal, especially after long-acting opioids.

ATLS 11th: Found-Down Opioid Patient

ATLS source check

ATLS Figure 1-1. Initial Assessment

Opioid poisoning often presents as an undifferentiated found-down patient. Apply xABCDE while treating reversible hypoventilation.

ATLS bedside change: Do not anchor on opioid intoxication: trauma, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, intracranial hemorrhage, and coingestion remain active until assessed.

Expose the patient for patches, injection sites, injury, hypothermia, and hidden packets. Naloxone response does not clear the cervical spine or rule out intracranial bleeding.

Disposition and Harm Reduction

Discharge only after stable mental status, normal ventilation, no recurrent sedation, no dangerous coingestion, and reliable follow-up. Long-acting opioids, repeated naloxone, infusion, body packing/stuffing, aspiration, pulmonary edema, suicidal ingestion, pregnancy, or pediatric exposure require extended observation or admission.

Rosen source check

Rosen reassessment after naloxone

Rosen emphasizes reassessment after antidote response: recurrence, pulmonary complications, aspiration, and co-ingestion clues determine disposition more than the fact that the patient woke up once.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli operationalizes naloxone dosing and observation; Rosen highlights the poisoned-patient reassessment loop before discharge.
Harm reduction: provide take-home naloxone, overdose education, and opioid-use-disorder treatment linkage when feasible.

Drug Dose Reference

InterventionDoseUseNotes
Naloxone low-dose IV0.04 mg IV, titrate upwardBreathing opioid-dependent patientGoal is ventilation, not full arousal.
Naloxone standard0.4 mg IV/IM/INModerate respiratory depressionRepeat every 2-3 min as needed.
Naloxone apnea/cyanosis2 mg IV/IN/IMApnea, cyanosis, severe hypoventilationBVM first/alongside naloxone.
Naloxone infusion~2/3 effective bolus per hourRecurrent respiratory depressionTitrate to respiratory status.
Whole bowel irrigationPEG 1-2 L/h adult PO/NGBody packer or massive sustained-release ingestionAirway protected.
BuprenorphineCommon ED start 4-8 mg SLModerate opioid withdrawal/OUDUse local protocol; avoid precipitated withdrawal.

Key Points

Ventilation first
  • Oxygen/BVM before and during naloxone.
Naloxone endpoint
  • Restore breathing, not necessarily wakefulness.
Rosen cross-check
  • Check mimics and coingestions if the story does not fit.
ATLS lens
  • Found-down patients still need xABCDE and trauma evaluation.

Inline MCQs

Inline board-style check
Q1. A found-down patient has coma, pinpoint pupils, and RR 5/min. Which action matters first?
  • A. A. Wait for urine tox confirmation
  • B. B. Ventilate with oxygen while preparing naloxone
  • C. C. Give activated charcoal
  • D. D. Discharge after observation
Incorrect. Urine testing does not guide immediate resuscitation.
Correct. Opioid poisoning kills through hypoventilation; oxygenation/ventilation comes first while naloxone is prepared.
Incorrect. Charcoal is unsafe before airway protection and is not the first move.
Incorrect. This patient is unstable.
Inline board-style check
Q2. Which naloxone strategy is best for a chronic opioid user who is breathing but somnolent?
  • A. A. 0.04 mg IV titrated upward
  • B. B. 10 mg IV immediately
  • C. C. No naloxone is ever safe
  • D. D. Flumazenil first
Correct. Titrate to ventilation and avoid abrupt withdrawal when the patient is still breathing.
Incorrect. Large boluses can precipitate vomiting, agitation, and withdrawal.
Incorrect. Naloxone is appropriate when ventilation is unsafe.
Incorrect. Flumazenil does not reverse opioids and can cause seizures in mixed overdose.
Inline board-style check
Q3. An apneic cyanotic adult with suspected heroin overdose is being bagged. Best initial naloxone dose?
  • A. A. 0.04 mg IV
  • B. B. 2 mg IV/IN/IM
  • C. C. 0.4 microgram IV
  • D. D. Withhold naloxone until CT head
Incorrect. This low dose is for a breathing opioid-dependent patient.
Correct. Apnea/cyanosis requires full reversal dosing while ventilation is underway.
Incorrect. This is not a useful resuscitation dose.
Incorrect. Do not delay reversal of respiratory failure.
Inline board-style check
Q4. Recurrent hypoventilation 40 minutes after naloxone most likely means:
  • A. A. Long-acting opioid outlasted naloxone
  • B. B. Naloxone caused opioid toxicity
  • C. C. The urine screen was false positive
  • D. D. Patient is cured
Correct. Naloxone duration can be shorter than methadone, fentanyl patch, sustained-release products, and packet leaks.
Incorrect. Naloxone is an antagonist.
Incorrect. The clinical recurrence after response is enough.
Incorrect. Recurrence requires repeat dosing/infusion and monitoring.
Inline board-style check
Q5. Which opioid is classically associated with seizures from a metabolite?
  • A. A. Meperidine
  • B. B. Morphine
  • C. C. Fentanyl
  • D. D. Oxycodone
Correct. Normeperidine can accumulate and cause seizures.
Incorrect. Morphine is not the classic metabolite-seizure answer.
Incorrect. Fentanyl causes apnea/rigidity more than metabolite seizures.
Incorrect. Oxycodone is not the classic answer.
Inline board-style check
Q6. Body packer management generally includes:
  • A. A. Endoscopic retrieval first
  • B. B. Whole bowel irrigation and monitoring if asymptomatic
  • C. C. Immediate discharge
  • D. D. Heat application to speed passage
Incorrect. Endoscopy risks packet rupture.
Correct. Packers intentionally transport many wrapped packets; WBI and monitoring are typical if asymptomatic.
Incorrect. Rupture can be fatal.
Incorrect. Heat is irrelevant and unsafe in patch exposure.
Inline board-style check
Q7. Which finding argues against simple opioid intoxication?
  • A. A. Bradypnea
  • B. B. Miosis
  • C. C. Dry hot skin with absent bowel sounds
  • D. D. Response to naloxone
Incorrect. Bradypnea fits opioids.
Incorrect. Miosis fits opioids but is not mandatory.
Correct. This points toward anticholinergic or mixed poisoning.
Incorrect. Response supports opioid effect.
Inline board-style check
Q8. Opioid withdrawal is suggested by:
  • A. A. Diarrhea, yawning, lacrimation, mydriasis
  • B. B. Bradypnea and coma
  • C. C. Miosis and hypothermia
  • D. D. Wide QRS
Correct. Withdrawal is adrenergic/GI activation.
Incorrect. This is intoxication.
Incorrect. This fits intoxication/mixed illness.
Incorrect. Think sodium-channel blocker or other coingestion.
